reason: The provided sources contain over 10 mutually verified facts about asteroid 2020 VT4's record-setting flyby, discovery timeline, physical characteristics, and orbital deflection.
story: On Friday the 13th of November 2020, a small asteroid named 2020 VT4 flew just 230 miles above Earth's surface over the South Pacific Ocean. Flying at virtually the same altitude as the International Space Station, it set the record for the closest known non-impacting asteroid pass in recorded history. Yet, no one on Earth saw it coming. Astronomers at the ATLAS survey in Hawaii only discovered the space rock 15 hours after its closest approach, as it was already zooming away into deep space. Because it approached from the direction of the Sun, ground-based telescopes were completely blinded to its arrival. Had the 5-to-10-meter rock struck our atmosphere, it would have mostly disintegrated into a brilliant meteor fireball and dropped scattered meteorites into the ocean. Instead, Earth's gravity yanked on the asteroid, bending its path and permanently shrinking its orbital period from 1.5 years down to just 10 months.
angle: On Friday the 13th, an asteroid skimmed just 230 miles above Earth—closer than the ISS—and astronomers didn't spot it until 15 hours after it passed.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2020 VT4 passed extremely close to Earth on Friday, November 13, 2020.
The asteroid skimmed less than 400 km (250 miles) above Earth's surface over the South Pacific Ocean.
It passed Earth at roughly the same altitude as the orbit of the International Space Station.
2020 VT4 set the record for the closest documented non-impacting asteroid pass of Earth.
Astronomers did not detect the asteroid until November 14, 2020, 15 hours after its closest approach.
The asteroid was discovered by the ATLAS survey at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii.
2020 VT4 is estimated to be roughly 5 to 10 meters (16 to 32 feet) in diameter.
Had it struck Earth, 2020 VT4 would have mostly disintegrated or burned up in the atmosphere.
If it had burned up in the atmosphere, it could have left behind a strewn field of meteorites.
Earth's gravity perturbed 2020 VT4's trajectory, shifting its orbit from an Apollo-type to an Aten-type orbit.
The encounter shortened the asteroid's orbital period around the Sun from about 1.5 years down to roughly 0.86 years.
2020 VT4 passed closer to Earth than asteroid 2020 QG, which passed about 3,000 km (1,864 miles) away earlier in 2020.

disputed: Exact flyby distance varies slightly across sources between 370 km (230 mi) and 383 km (238 mi); script should attribute or phrase as under 400 km (250 miles).
